slides.title: A cost-segregation study can pull deductions into year one, but only your CPA can say if they count
slides.subtitle: Resource SR.3. Cost segregation & tax-impact estimator
meta: Education only. Not tax advice. Your CPA decides every input and result.
slides.notes:
This deck teaches you how to use one tool: the cost segregation and tax-impact estimator. It's a scenario workbook for one property.

It estimates how much depreciation a cost-segregation study might move into year one, and what that could mean for your tax. I built it for the conversation with your CPA. It doesn't replace that conversation.

We'll start with what a study does, and the whole calculation in plain numbers. Then each tab, the inputs, the formulas, and the rules built into it. Then the common mistakes, the low and high cases, the evidence to ask a study provider for, and how to hand it to your CPA.

One warning up front. Whether any of this applies depends on the property, the dates, and how you use it. It also depends on your participation, your income, and the tax year. The workbook makes those inputs visible. Your CPA decides them.

slides.title: A study moves part of the building into short lives you can deduct in year one
slides.text: A cost-segregation study splits the building into parts, so some of it can be deducted in year one instead of over 27.5 or 39 years.
slides.support: Cedar Ridge (hypothetical): a $385,000 lake house owned by Maya and Chris. In the base case the study adds about $67,000 of year-one deduction, if they can use it.
slides.notes:
In plain words: when you buy a rental, you can't deduct the building's cost all at once. You deduct it a slice at a time over 27.5 or 39 years. That paper write-off for wear on the building is depreciation. Land is never depreciated.

A cost-segregation study splits the building into parts. Some parts, such as land improvements, qualify for 5-, 7-, or 15-year lives. When bonus depreciation, an extra first-year deduction, applies, those short-life parts and your furniture can be deducted in full in year one.

Our running example is Cedar Ridge, a hypothetical three-bedroom lake house. Maya and Chris, a two-earner household with about $185,000 of W-2 income, bought it for $385,000 and furnished it for $32,000. In the base case, a study adds about $67,000 of year-one deduction. At a 32% rate, that's about $21,000 before a $4,500 fee. That only holds if the loss is usable this year.

First, the whole calculation in plain numbers. Then we'll build the workbook that does it.

slides.title: Worked by hand, Cedar Ridge's base case gives a $107,072 year-1 deduction
slides.side:
Rest of building: $312,800 − $68,816 = $243,984.

At 32%, the illustrative tax effect is **$34,263**, only if all of it is usable this year.

Base uses a full first year for simplicity. With a June start and the mid-month convention, the building line is $3,389.
slides.notes:
Here's the whole calculation for Cedar Ridge's base case, worked by hand. The workbook we build next does exactly this.

Basis is $385,000 plus $6,000 of capitalized costs, or $391,000. Land at 20% is $78,200, and land never depreciates. The building is $312,800.

The study moves 22% of the building into short lives. That's $68,816, which leaves $243,984 of remaining building.

Accelerated depreciation is the reclassified parts plus the $32,000 of furnishings, at 100% bonus. That's $100,816, if eligible. Ordinary depreciation is $243,984 divided by 39, or $6,256. Add them and the year-one deduction is $107,072.

Two honest caveats. The base takes a full first year to keep the math simple. With a June start, the building line is closer to $3,389. And the $34,263 tax effect at 32% only holds if all of the deduction is usable this year. Every figure here is a Cedar Ridge assumption.

slides.title: The workbook does four jobs, and none of them is deciding your tax
slides.text: Use it after Sam's PA.5 lesson. No property yet? Practice with the Cedar Ridge inputs.
items: Collects every input a CPA will ask for, with a source and a status beside each.
Separates ordinary depreciation from accelerated depreciation, so you see what the study changes.
Shows the tax effect only after the loss limits you enter, so an unusable deduction never looks like cash.
Lists every assumption still unverified, so nothing gets treated as settled by accident.
slides.notes:
The workbook does four jobs.

First, it collects every input a CPA will ask for, with a source and a status beside each one. Second, it separates ordinary depreciation from accelerated depreciation. That way you can see what the study actually changes, compared with doing nothing.

Third, and this is the one people skip, it shows the tax effect only after the loss limits you enter. A big deduction you can't use this year is not cash this year. The workbook won't let it look like cash.

Fourth, it lists every assumption that's still unverified.

Sam's PA.5 lesson walks through a study in more depth. Use this workbook after that, when you have a real address and a real quote from a study provider. No property yet? Build it anyway and enter the Cedar Ridge inputs. If you get the same numbers I just showed you, your formulas work.

slides.title: Five tabs keep inputs, formulas, and results apart, and only inputs take typing
rows: Every assumption, with what to enter, source, status, and date checked
The separated results and open items you bring to the CPA
Low, base, and high side by side
Every rule the workbook relies on, with link and date

box.label: Status values, used everywhere
box.text: **Verified** (document in hand). **CPA to supply.** **Unverified** (estimate or placeholder). **Study** (from the cost-segregation report). **Example input** (teaching figure).

slides.notes:
Build it as a spreadsheet with five tabs. You build it from the tables in this lesson. The formulas use these tab names and cell addresses, so keep them exactly.

Inputs holds every assumption. Calc holds formulas only, and nobody types there. Outputs holds the separated results you bring to your CPA, plus the open items. Scenarios puts low, base, and high cases side by side. And Sources lists every rule the workbook relies on, with a link and a date.

Shade the input cells. Those are the only cells anyone types into. Rows 1 and 2 hold the title and headers. Don't insert heading rows, or every address shifts.

The status column uses the same values everywhere. Verified means you have the document in hand. CPA to supply means it's their call. Unverified means it's an estimate or a placeholder. Study means it comes from the cost-segregation report. In the Cedar Ridge example you'll also see Example input. That marks a teaching figure a real owner would pull from reports and mark Verified.

slides.title: Section 1 records dates and basis, and the contract date matters as much as closing
slides.caption: B3 to B5 hold the address, the owners and entity (PA.10), and the tax year. B12 names the land method.
slides.notes:
The Inputs tab has five sections. Column A is the field and column B is the value. The next columns hold what to enter, the source, the status, and the date checked. The values here are the Cedar Ridge base case. All of them are assumptions for teaching.

Section 1 is property and dates. Notice there are three dates, not one. The binding contract date, the closing date, and the placed-in-service date. The contract date matters because the IRS treats property as acquired no later than the day a binding written contract was signed. A contract signed on or before January 19, 2025 can change the bonus rate, even if you closed later.

Placed in service means the date the property was ready and available for rent. Your listing's live date and first available night help. Your CPA confirms it.

Then the money: purchase price, capitalized closing costs, the land share, improvements before first rental, furnishings, and the study fee. The land share is Unverified until your CPA picks a method, like the assessor ratio, an appraisal, or the study.
slides.text: The contract date matters because a contract signed on or before Jan. 19, 2025 can change the bonus rate.

slides.title: Sections 2 and 3 take the study's split and screen the bonus rate by date
slides.caption: 15% + 0% + 7% = 22%, the Cedar Ridge base case. Once you have the report, replace them with the study's dollars divided by building basis.
slides.notes:
Section 2 holds the study results. B17, B18, and B19 are the shares of the building the study moves into 5-year, 7-year, and 15-year property. For Cedar Ridge they're 15%, 0%, and 7%. Those add to 22%, the Cedar Ridge base case. The 15-year bucket is often land improvements. A recovery period is just the number of years the tax rules spread a cost over.

These are placeholders until you have a report. Then you replace them with the study's dollar figures divided by the building basis.

B20 is the recovery period for the rest of the building, 27.5 or 39 years. That's your CPA's call, and we'll see why in the rules.

Section 3 is bonus depreciation. B21 is a formula, not a typed number, so don't type in it. It checks whether the contract, closing, and placed-in-service dates all fall after January 19, 2025. If they do, it shows 100%. If not, it shows the word CPA. If your CPA gives a different rate or an election, it goes in B22.

slides.title: Sections 4 and 5 capture use, hours, and loss limits, the inputs that decide usability
rows: Days rented at a fair rental price
Number of stays / days in all rental periods
Participation test relied on / real estate professional
Share of year-1 loss usable this year
Switches: full first year / divide by rental use
slides.notes:
Section 4 is use, participation, and loss limits. These are the inputs that decide whether a deduction becomes cash this year.

Days rented, stays, and days in all rental periods come from your platform and property management software reports. For Cedar Ridge I've used 212 days and 61 stays, marked Example input. Personal-use days come from your calendar. Maya and Chris plan about 10.

B27 and B28 ask for your hours and everyone else's: the cleaner, the co-host, the manager. Keep a log as you go.

Then the CPA cells: participation test, professional status, MAGI, the usable share, and the rates. Look at B32. The base case sets the usable share to 100%. That assumes your CPA rules the whole loss usable, and the hours aren't even logged yet. It's the biggest open assumption in the example. We'll see the case where it fails.

Section 5 has two switches. B35 picks a full first year, for simplicity, or the mid-month fraction. B36 turns on dividing expenses by rental days. The base case uses neither.
slides.text: Base case assumes your CPA rules the whole loss usable (B32 = 100%). The hours aren't logged yet.
slides.caption: Base case assumes the CPA rules the whole loss usable (B32 = 100%). Hours aren't logged yet. The passive case later shows what happens if it isn't.

slides.title: The Calc tab keeps land out of every depreciation line below cell B5
rows: CPA override (Inputs B22) if entered; else date screen (Inputs B21); else 0
Year-1 total (Calc B19) × rental-use fraction (Calc B20)
slides.caption: Calc B14 and B15 cover any bonus rate under 100% (the CPA's software computes B15). Calc B17 is the first-year fraction; Calc B18 applies it; Calc B20 is the rental-use fraction (not Inputs B20, the building life).
slides.notes:
The Calc tab is formulas only. Each row is one cell in column B. Calc and Inputs both use column B, so I'll always say which tab. On this slide, a plain B number is a Calc cell.

Start with basis, your cost for tax purposes: price plus capitalized costs plus early improvements. That's $391,000 for Cedar Ridge. B4 and B5 are the heart of the land rule. No formula below B5 touches the land in B4.

The study's shares move $68,816 of the building into short lives, leaving $243,984. Add the furnishings and you get $100,816 of bonus-eligible basis.

Look at B12. If your CPA entered an override, it uses that. If the date screen returned a number, it uses that. Otherwise it falls back to zero, on purpose.

The remaining building runs straight-line, the same amount each year: $6,256 over 39 years. Year one in the base case is $107,072. B14 and B15 only matter when bonus is under 100%. Don't estimate those by hand.

slides.title: The lower Calc rows apply the flags, the usable share, and the no-study comparison
rows: Shows the Pub 925 message when the average stay is 7 days or less
Tests personal days against the greater of 14 or 10% of rented days
Furnishings bonus + building at B20 years
slides.caption: Calc B31 is the added tax effect from the study ($21,456). Calc B33 and B34 carry the accelerated ($100,816) and straight-line ($6,256) pools to the Outputs tab.
slides.notes:
The lower half of the Calc tab turns a deduction into something you can reason about.

B22 divides days in all rental periods by the number of stays. For Cedar Ridge that's 3.48 days. B23 flags an average stay of 7 days or less, which sends your CPA to a specific Publication 925 test. B24 runs the home-use day test.

Then the money. B25 multiplies the deduction by the usable share your CPA enters. Whatever isn't usable lands in B26 as carried forward or suspended. B27 applies the rates. That's $34,263 in the base case, only if every input holds.

B29 is the comparison I care most about: year one with no study at all. Furniture still gets bonus, and the whole building runs straight-line. That's $40,021. So B30, the study's added deduction, is $67,051.

B32 is adjusted basis after year one, $315,928. That's the starting point for any future gain.

slides.title: The Outputs tab keeps ordinary, accelerated, and usable amounts on separate lines
rows: Bonus on reclassified parts and furnishings
Not lost, but not cash this year
Starting point for any future gain
Tax that may come due on these amounts when you sell (OP.12)

box.label: Top line of the tab, in bold
box.text: Illustrative only. Every figure depends on inputs your CPA has not yet confirmed. Not tax advice.

slides.notes:
The Outputs tab is what you bring to the CPA. Keep these lines separate. And never add the tax effect to your operating cash flow in another model. It's an estimate, not income.

Ordinary depreciation is $6,256. Accelerated is $100,816. Together that's a $107,072 estimated deduction, before loss limits. Then usable this year, and carried forward. In the base case all of it is usable, but that's an assumption your CPA has to confirm.

The tax effect is labeled illustrative for a reason. It's $34,263 only if every input holds.

The two pools at the bottom matter later. In plain words, when you sell, part of the depreciation you took can be taxed. That's called recapture. The accelerated pool is mostly section 1245 items, with ordinary-income recapture exposure. The straight-line pool is unrecaptured section 1250 exposure, taxed at a maximum 25%. OP.12 picks both up.

Put the disclaimer line at the top of the tab in bold. The tab also lists the flags and every input that isn't Verified.

slides.title: Five built-in rules decide whether the deduction can count this year

gates.q: Were all three dates after Jan. 19, 2025?
Is the asset short-life property, 20 years or less?
Are personal days at or under the greater of 14 or 10% of rented days?
Is the average stay 7 days or less?
gates.sub: Cedar Ridge: 212 ÷ 61 = 3.48 days. Under Pub 925, that isn't a 'rental activity', so the participation tests in gate 5 decide.

gates.q: After participation tests and loss limits, is the loss usable?

slides.end: All five clear: tax effect = usable deduction × CPA's rates.
slides.notes:
The lesson lists eight rules. Five of them work like yes-or-no gates, and they're on this slide. The next slide covers the other three, plus a closer look at the loss limits.

Gate one is dates. The IRS says 100% bonus is now permanent for eligible property acquired after January 19, 2025. A binding contract signed on or before that date can change the answer, even if you closed later. That's why Inputs B6 exists. The screen only checks dates. Your CPA confirms eligibility.

Gate two: bonus needs a recovery period of 20 years or less. The building's 27.5 or 39 years is too long, and land isn't depreciable at all.

Gate three is the Publication 527 home-use test. Cedar Ridge's 10 personal days sit under 21.2.

Gate four is Publication 925's average-stay rule. At 3.48 days, Cedar Ridge isn't a rental activity under that rule. That's not bad news. It means the participation tests decide.

Gate five matters most. Your CPA sets the usable share in Inputs B32. If it's zero, the whole deduction carries forward and this year's tax effect is zero.

slides.title: Three more rules set the building life, late-study filings, and basis
items: Building life is a CPA call: 39 years if short stays count as transient use, 27.5 if not. At 27.5, Cedar Ridge's line is $8,872, not $6,256.
Gate five, up close: the $25,000 allowance is gone by $150,000 of MAGI, so it doesn't help Maya and Chris at about $185,000.
A study on property placed in service in an earlier year can need Form 3115 (a change in accounting method) with a one-time catch-up adjustment.
Depreciation reduces basis whether or not you claim it. The Outputs tab carries both pools to OP.12.
slides.notes:
Here are the other three rules, plus a closer look at gate five.

The building life. Publication 946 defines residential rental property by where the income comes from. It excludes hotel, motel, or inn units used mostly on a transient basis. How that applies to a house rented for short stays is a question for your CPA. The Cedar Ridge base case uses 39 years, the cautious choice. At 27.5, its line would be $8,872 a year.

Now gate five. Publication 925 describes a special allowance of up to $25,000 for active participation. It phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of MAGI. At Maya and Chris's assumed $185,000, it doesn't help them either way. The excess business loss limit was $313,000, or $626,000 joint, for 2025, far above their $107,072.

A late study can need Form 3115, a change in accounting method. Your CPA handles that filing.

And depreciation reduces basis whether or not you claim it. That's why the pools carry forward.

slides.title: Six mistakes turn an honest estimate into a number that looks like cash
items: Adding the tax effect to operating cash flow or to a lender's math. It's a one-time estimate, not income.
Treating the estimated deduction as cash before the CPA sets the usable share.
Typing into the Calc tab. Only the shaded input cells take typing.
Guessing a CPA cell instead of leaving it blank and marking its status.
Applying bonus to land or to the whole building. Land never depreciates.
Counting furniture twice: once in Inputs B14 and again inside the study.
slides.notes:
Now that you've seen the rules, here are the mistakes this workbook is built to catch.

The biggest is mixing the tax effect into cash flow. Don't add it to operating cash flow in another model. It's a one-time estimate that depends on your CPA's rulings, not income the property earns. And keep it out of lender math. A lender underwrites cash flow, not deductions.

Second, treating the deduction as cash before your CPA sets the usable share. If the activity is passive, that share can be zero.

Third, typing into the Calc tab. Once someone overwrites a formula, nobody can trust the outputs.

Fourth, guessing. If a cell is your CPA's call, leave it blank and mark it CPA to supply.

Fifth, bonus on land or on the whole building. Bonus applies to the short-life pieces only.

Sixth, counting furniture twice. If your furnishings are already on your books in Inputs B14, ask the study provider how they treated them.

slides.title: Land and reclass shares alone swing the year-1 deduction from $79,020 to $137,670
rows: Illustrative tax effect at 32%, if usable
slides.caption: Only two inputs change. Low and high land on the same remaining building by coincidence, not by rule.
slides.notes:
This is the Scenarios tab. The low and high columns change only two inputs: the land share and the reclassified share of the building. Everything else stays at the base values.

In the low case, land is 30% and the study moves 15% of the building. The year-one deduction is $79,020. In the high case, land is 15% and the study moves 30%. The deduction is $137,670.

That's a wide range from two inputs. It tells you where to spend your questions. Ask your CPA how the land share will be set, and ask the study provider how they support the reclass share.

Notice the last row. The bigger the year-one deduction, the lower your adjusted basis. In the high case, basis drops to $285,330. That feeds straight into the gain at sale in OP.12.

And a small note: low and high happen to land on the same remaining-building figure, $232,645. That's a coincidence of these two inputs.

slides.title: The passive case is the one to fear: $107,072 of deduction, $0 of tax effect this year
slides.text: Illustrative tax effect at 32%. Each row changes one thing from the base case.

items.label: Mid-month, placed in service in June
Passive, no loss usable this year

slides.caption: The study adds $67,051 of year-1 deduction over no study: $21,456 at 32%, or $16,956 after the $4,500 fee, if fully usable. In the passive case, $107,072 carries forward.
slides.notes:
Now the adjustments your CPA is likely to raise. Each bar changes one thing from the base case.

Mid-month convention, placed in service in June: the building gets 6.5 months, $3,389 instead of $6,256. The tax effect drops to $33,346. Dividing expenses by rental use, 212 out of 222 days, drops it to $32,720.

No study at all: furniture still gets bonus, because it's short-life property either way. That's $12,807.

And the passive case. If no loss is usable this year, the tax effect this year is zero. The deduction isn't lost. It waits. Remember, the base bar assumes the usable share is 100%. With the allowance phased out at their income, that depends on the participation tests.

The study adds $67,051 of year-one deduction over no study. At 32% that's $21,456, or $16,956 after the fee, if fully usable. It mostly shifts timing, and it lowers your basis faster, which shows up at sale.

slides.title: Studies have no set standards, so get twelve pieces of evidence in writing

left.head: From IRS Pub 5653
items: Preparer's name, credentials, and experience
Every participant and their role
Name and description of the method
Reconciliation to price and basis
Source of plans, or site-visit notes and photos

right.head: To fit this workbook
items: Asset-by-asset schedule with class and life
Legal reasoning for each classification
Land allocation method and support
How furnishings on your books were treated
Placed-in-service date the study assumed
Discussion of recapture at sale
Fee, delivery date, and IRS support

slides.notes:
The IRS publishes a Cost Segregation Audit Techniques Guide for its own examiners. It's Publication 5653, and the current version is dated February 2025.

It says there are no standards for preparing these studies. It says they vary widely in method, documentation, depth, and preparer expertise. It contrasts a detailed engineering approach built on actual cost records with survey, letter, and rule-of-thumb approaches.

Its principal elements of a quality study include a preparer with expertise and experience, and a reconciliation of allocated costs to actual costs. Its information requests ask who prepared the study, what role each person played, and where the blueprints came from.

So use that guide to shape what you ask for. The left column comes straight from it. The right column is my recommendations for making the study fit this workbook. The asset schedule fills Inputs B17 to B19. The land method ties to B11. The placed-in-service date must match B8. Get all twelve in writing before you engage the provider.

slides.title: Hand the workbook to your CPA in five steps, dates and basis first
items: Before the meeting, fill every input you can document. Leave CPA cells blank.
Send the workbook, statement, receipts, study quote, day calendar, and hour log.
In the meeting, go in order: dates and basis, methods, participation, limits, rates.
Rerun Scenarios, save a dated copy, and log the CPA's name and date on Sources.
Decide on the study after seeing the added deduction, passive case, and fee.

box.label: A script for the meeting
box.text: Here is my estimate and every assumption behind it. Which inputs are wrong, which apply to me, and what would you enter instead?

slides.notes:
Here's how to use this with a CPA.

Before the meeting, fill in every input you can document. Leave the CPA cells blank rather than guessing. Mark each status honestly.

Send the workbook with the settlement statement, the furnishing receipts, the study quote, and your calendar of rental and personal days.

In the meeting, go in order. Dates and basis first: placed in service, capitalized costs, land method, building life. Then method choices: the bonus rate or election, the first-year convention, and the rental-use division. Then participation and limits, with your hour log. Then the tax rates.

Afterward, rerun the Scenarios tab with their inputs. Save a dated copy. On the Sources tab, add a row each time your CPA confirms an input, with their name and the date. An email counts. That row matters more than any IRS link on the tab. Keep the copy with your tax records for OP.12.

And if you're not sure how to open the conversation, read them the script on this slide.

slides.title: For Cedar Ridge, twelve groups of inputs are still open, and Outputs lists every one
items: Address, owners, tax year (B3 to B5)
Contract, closing, in-service dates (B6 to B8)
Capitalized acquisition costs of $6,000 (B10)
Land share of 20% and its method (B11, B12)
Study fee, provider, and split (B15 to B19)
Building life, 39 vs 27.5 years (B20)
Bonus eligibility and any election (B21, B22)
Rental days and stays (B23, B25, B26)
Personal days, expense division (B24, B36)
Hours and participation (B27 to B30)
MAGI, usable share, tax rates (B31 to B34)
First-year convention (B35)
slides.notes:
This is the open list. The Outputs tab filters the Inputs tab for every status that isn't Verified. For the Cedar Ridge teaching example, it comes out to these twelve groups. Every cell here is on the Inputs tab.

Look at how much is on it. Who owns it and the tax year. The dates that drive the bonus rate. The capitalized costs. The land share and method. The study fee, provider, and the reclass split. The building life. Bonus eligibility. The rental days and stays, which are example inputs until real reports replace them. Personal days and whether expenses are divided. Hours, the participation test, and professional status. MAGI, the usable share, and the rates. And the first-year convention.

That's almost every input that moves the answer. So the $34,263 on the Outputs tab sits on top of all twelve open questions.

That's the honest state of any estimate before the CPA meeting. The goal of the meeting is to shrink this list. Each item your CPA confirms comes off.

slides.title: Four steps this week get the workbook ready for your CPA meeting
items: Build the five tabs. No property yet? Enter Cedar Ridge and check you get $107,072 and $34,263. Have one? Enter what you can document.
Mark every input's status: Verified, CPA to supply, Unverified, or Study.
Ask one study provider for a written quote and the twelve-item evidence list.
Send your CPA the workbook, statement, receipts, and calendar.

slides.title: Every rule in the workbook traces to an IRS publication, notice, or form

items.title: IRS: guidance on the additional first-year depreciation deduction (One, Big, Beautiful Bill)
IRS Notice 2026-11
items.note: Interim guidance; binding written contract rule

items.title: IRS Publication 946
items.note: 20-year limit for bonus; land; rates by date; transient exclusion; mid-month

items.title: IRS Publication 527
items.note: Personal-use day test; expense division; allowable depreciation

items.title: IRS Publication 925
items.note: 7-day rule; participation tests; $25,000 allowance and phase-out

items.title: IRS: About Form 3115
items.note: Change in accounting method for late studies

items.title: IRS Publication 5653, Cost Segregation Audit Techniques Guide
items.note: No standards; methods; quality elements; information requests

slides.notes:
These are the sources the workbook relies on.

The IRS news release and Notice 2026-11 cover the permanent 100% bonus after January 19, 2025. They also cover the binding contract rule and the 40% election. Publication 946 covers the 20-year limit, the land rule, the rates by date, the residential rental definition, and the mid-month convention.

Publication 527 covers the personal-use day test and allowable depreciation. Publication 925 covers the 7-day rule, the participation tests, and the $25,000 allowance. The Form 461 instructions give the 2025 excess business loss thresholds. Form 3115 covers late studies. Publication 5653 is the examiners' guide to cost-segregation studies. Publication 544 and Topic 409 cover what happens at sale.

The Cedar Ridge figures come from the course's hypothetical teaching example. The low and high cases, the study fee, the reclass split, and the adjustments are new assumptions for teaching. Tax rules change by year, so check each one with your CPA.
